deck.title: DynamoDB
deck.analogy: DynamoDB is a stadium coat-check: one ticket number takes you straight to one hook, never a search, whether there are 500 coats or 5 million.

subtopics.title: DynamoDB vs RDS — the first fork in every question
Capacity modes — same logic as EC2 pricing

cards.front: What is DynamoDB and what is its signature performance promise?

back.answer: AWS's serverless NoSQL database with single-digit millisecond latency at ANY scale.
back.explanation: Every lookup goes straight to a key, never a search, so 10 or 10 million requests/sec run at the same speed.
back.mnemonic: Coat-check: one ticket, one hook, one grab.

cards.front: What do 'serverless' and 'NoSQL' mean in DynamoDB?

back.answer: Serverless: no servers to size, patch or connect to. NoSQL: items with flexible attributes, no joins, no rigid schema.
back.explanation: You just call an API; each item can have different attributes.

cards.front: DynamoDB vs RDS/Aurora: which fits joins, complex queries and an existing SQL app?

back.explanation: Relational schema, joins and complex queries point to RDS/Aurora.

cards.sourceHeading: DynamoDB vs RDS — the first fork in every question

cards.front: DynamoDB vs RDS: which fits massive scale, serverless, key-value, millisecond latency, unpredictable growth?

back.explanation: Key-value lookups at any scale with no servers to manage.

cards.sourceHeading: DynamoDB vs RDS — the first fork in every question

cards.front: Trap: a question says 'migrate with no code changes from MySQL'. Is DynamoDB the answer?

back.answer: No — RDS/Aurora. DynamoDB is NoSQL and would require rewriting queries.
back.explanation: MySQL compatibility means a relational engine.

cards.sourceHeading: DynamoDB vs RDS — the first fork in every question

cards.front: What are the DynamoDB partition key and sort key for?

back.answer: Partition key determines which physical partition stores the item; the optional sort key orders items within a partition.
back.explanation: E.g. one customer can have many orders sorted by date.

cards.front: What is a DynamoDB hot partition and how do you avoid it?

back.answer: One partition takes most traffic and throttles; avoid it with a high-cardinality partition key like user_id or order_id.
back.explanation: Data is spread by hashing the partition key; low-cardinality keys (status, country, date) concentrate traffic.

cards.front: When is DynamoDB Provisioned capacity mode the right choice?

back.answer: Steady, predictable traffic; it's cheaper, and auto scaling can flex within bounds.
back.explanation: Like the Reserved-Instance instinct.

cards.sourceHeading: Capacity modes — same logic as EC2 pricing

cards.front: When is DynamoDB On-Demand capacity mode the right choice?

back.answer: Spiky, unpredictable or brand-new workloads; pay per request with no planning.
back.explanation: E.g. flash sales or new apps with unknown traffic.

cards.sourceHeading: Capacity modes — same logic as EC2 pricing

cards.front: Trap: a DynamoDB app gets throttled during unpredictable traffic spikes. What's the fix?

back.answer: Switch to On-Demand mode; don't over-provision.
back.explanation: Pay-per-request absorbs spikes.

cards.sourceHeading: Capacity modes — same logic as EC2 pricing

cards.front: What does 1 DynamoDB RCU buy?

back.answer: 1 strongly consistent read/sec, or 2 eventually consistent reads/sec, for items ≤ 4 KB.
back.explanation: Eventual consistency is half price because it may serve a slightly stale copy.

cards.front: What does 1 DynamoDB WCU buy?

back.answer: 1 write per second for an item ≤ 1 KB.

cards.front: How do you make DynamoDB always return the latest write, and what's the default?

back.answer: Request a strongly consistent read; the default is eventually consistent.

cards.front: What is DAX for DynamoDB?

back.answer: In-memory cache for DynamoDB: microsecond reads, API-compatible (zero code changes), works only with DynamoDB.
back.explanation: For caching other stores or code-level flexibility, use ElastiCache.

cards.front: What are DynamoDB Global Tables and how do they differ from Aurora Global Database?

back.answer: Multi-region active-active: read and write locally in each region. Aurora Global has one writer region.
back.explanation: Global Tables requires Streams enabled.

cards.front: What are DynamoDB Streams and how long are changes kept?

back.answer: A change feed of every insert/update/delete, kept 24 hours, typically triggering Lambda.

cards.front: How does DynamoDB TTL work, what does it cost, and how precise is it?

back.answer: Expiry timestamp attribute; items auto-deleted free (no WCU) within ~48 hours of expiry.
back.explanation: Classic use: session data, temp tokens.

cards.front: What is a DynamoDB GSI?

back.answer: Index to query by a different attribute; can be added anytime and has its own capacity.
back.explanation: E.g. query by email when the key is user_id.

cards.front: Trap: a DynamoDB table already exists and needs another query path. Is LSI correct?

back.answer: No — an LSI can only be created at table creation; pick GSI.
back.explanation: LSI gives an alternate sort key with the same partition key.

cards.front: What are DynamoDB Transactions and their cost?

back.answer: ACID all-or-nothing across multiple items/tables, costing 2x the capacity.

cards.front: What does DynamoDB PITR provide?

back.answer: Continuous backup; restore to any second in the last 35 days.

cards.front: What is the classic fully serverless web/API stack ending in DynamoDB?

back.answer: User → CloudFront → API Gateway → Lambda → DynamoDB.
back.explanation: CDN, front door, code, data.
back.code: User → CloudFront → API Gateway → Lambda → DynamoDB

cards.front: What is the DynamoDB item size limit and the workaround for larger objects?

back.answer: 400 KB; store the object in S3 and keep the S3 pointer in DynamoDB.

cards.front: A flash sale causes unpredictable spikes and the DynamoDB table throttles. Best fix?

back.explanation: Pay-per-request absorbs spikes.

choices.text: Provisioned mode with higher fixed capacity

choices.why: Adds query paths, not spike capacity.

cards.front: Reduce DynamoDB read latency to microseconds without changing application code. Which?

back.explanation: API-compatible cache, DynamoDB-only.

choices.why: API-compatible in-memory cache, zero code changes.

cards.front: Global users need low-latency reads AND writes in every region on DynamoDB. Which?

back.explanation: Active-active; Aurora Global has only one writer.

cards.front: Run custom logic whenever DynamoDB items are added or modified. Which?

back.explanation: 24-hour change feed triggers functions.

choices.why: Change feed triggers functions on item changes.

cards.front: Automatically remove session records after 30 minutes at no cost in DynamoDB. Which?

back.explanation: Free auto-delete, ~48h window.

cards.front: DynamoDB table keyed on user_id must also be queried by email. Which?

back.explanation: Addable anytime; LSI is creation-time only.

choices.why: Cache, not a new query key.

cards.front: Debit one account and credit another in DynamoDB — both or neither. Which?

back.explanation: ACID, 2x capacity cost.

cards.front: Store 2 MB documents per record with DynamoDB metadata. Best design?

back.answer: S3 for the object, DynamoDB holds the pointer.
back.explanation: 400 KB item limit.

cards.front: A DynamoDB application must always see the most recent write. Which?

back.explanation: 1 RCU vs 2 eventual reads.

cards.front: Reporting needs joins across many tables. Which database?

back.explanation: Relational = SQL.
